The United States-based scientific agency classifies all landmasses (including all continental [mainlands](/wiki/Mainland "Mainland") except Antarctica) surrounded by water as islands. Under their definition, Africa, Australia, [Eurasia](/wiki/Eurasia "Eurasia"), North America, and South America are classified as continental mainland islands.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Three_Gorges_dam.jpg/250px-Three_Gorges_dam.jpg)](/wiki/File:Three_Gorges_dam.jpg)

The Three Gorges Dam in 2006

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Yangtze_longitudinal_profile_upstream.JPG/250px-Yangtze_longitudinal_profile_upstream.JPG)](/wiki/File:Yangtze_longitudinal_profile_upstream.JPG)

Diagram showing dams planned for the upper reaches of the Yangtze River

As of 2007, there are two dams built on the Yangtze River: [Three Gorges Dam](/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam "Three Gorges Dam") and [Gezhouba Dam](/wiki/Gezhouba_Dam "Gezhouba Dam"). The Three Gorges Dam is the [largest power station in the world](/wiki/List_of_largest_power_stations "List of largest power stations") by installed capacity, at 22.5 GW. Several dams are operating or are being constructed on the upper portion of the river, the [Jinsha River](/wiki/Jinsha_River "Jinsha River"). Among them, the [Baihetan Dam](/wiki/Baihetan_Dam "Baihetan Dam") is the second largest after the Three Gorges Dam, and the [Xiluodu Dam](/wiki/Xiluodu_Dam "Xiluodu Dam") is the 4th largest power station in the world.

A topographic map of China

China's landscape is vast and diverse, ranging from the [Gobi](/wiki/Gobi_Desert "Gobi Desert") and [Taklamakan Deserts](/wiki/Taklamakan_Desert "Taklamakan Desert") in the arid north to the [subtropical](/wiki/Subtropical "Subtropical") forests in the wetter south. The [Himalaya](/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya"), [Karakoram](/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), [Pamir](/wiki/Pamir_Mountains "Pamir Mountains") and [Tian Shan](/wiki/Tian_Shan "Tian Shan") mountain ranges separate China from much of [South](/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") and [Central Asia](/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia"). The [Yangtze](/wiki/Yangtze_River "Yangtze River") and Yellow Rivers, the third- and sixth-longest in the world, respectively, run from the [Tibetan Plateau](/wiki/Tibetan_Plateau "Tibetan Plateau") to the densely populated eastern seaboard. China's coastline along the [Pacific Ocean](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") is 14,500 km (9,000 mi) long and is bounded by the [Bohai](/wiki/Bohai_Sea "Bohai Sea"), [Yellow](/wiki/Yellow_Sea "Yellow Sea"), [East China](/wiki/East_China_Sea "East China Sea") and [South China](/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea") seas. China connects through the Kazakh border to the [Eurasian Steppe](/wiki/Eurasian_Steppe "Eurasian Steppe").

Hong Kong :: History :: Prehistory and Imperial China :: chunk_0008
The earliest known human traces in what is now called Hong Kong are dated by some to 35,000-39,000 years ago during the [Paleolithic](/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic") period. The claim is based on an archaeological investigation in [Wong Tei Tung](/wiki/Wong_Tei_Tung "Wong Tei Tung") in the [Sai Kung Peninsula](/wiki/Sai_Kung_Peninsula "Sai Kung Peninsula") in 2003. The archaeological works revealed [knapped](/wiki/Knapping "Knapping") [stone tools](/wiki/Stone_tool "Stone tool") from deposits dated by optical [luminescence dating](/wiki/Luminescence_dating "Luminescence dating").[[32]](#cite_note-38)

During the Middle [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period, about 6,000 years ago, the region had been widely occupied by humans.[[33]](#cite_note-Meacham2-39) Neolithic to [Bronze Age](/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") Hong Kong settlers were semi-coastal people. Early inhabitants are believed to have been [Austronesians](/wiki/Austronesian_peoples "Austronesian peoples") in the Middle Neolithic period, and later the [Yue](/wiki/Baiyue "Baiyue") people.[[33]](#cite_note-Meacham2-39) As hinted by the archaeological works in Sha Ha, Sai Kung, rice cultivation had been introduced since the [Late Neolithic](/wiki/Late_Neolithic "Late Neolithic") period.[[34]](#cite_note-Li38-40) Bronze Age Hong Kong featured coarse pottery, hard pottery, quartz and stone jewelry, as well as small bronze implements.[[33]](#cite_note-Meacham2-39)

The [Afriski resort](/wiki/Afriski "Afriski") in the [Maloti Mountains](/wiki/Maloti_Mountains "Maloti Mountains")

Lesotho covers 30,355 km2 (11,720 sq mi). It is the only independent state in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 metres (3,281 ft) in elevation. Its lowest point of 1,400 metres (4,593 ft) is thus the [highest lowest point of any country in the world](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_lowest_point "List of countries by lowest point"). Over 80% of the country lies above 1,800 metres (5,906 ft). Lesotho is the southernmost landlocked country in the world. It is the largest of the world's [three independent states completely surrounded by the territory of another country](/wiki/List_of_countries_that_border_only_one_other_country#Landlocked "List of countries that border only one other country"), with [Vatican City](/wiki/Vatican_City "Vatican City") and [San Marino](/wiki/San_Marino "San Marino") being the other two. It is the only such state outside the Italian peninsula and [Europe](/wiki/Europe "Europe"), as well as the only one that is not a [microstate](/wiki/Microstate "Microstate").

Lesotho lies between latitudes [28°](/wiki/28th_parallel_south "28th parallel south") and [31°S](/wiki/31st_parallel_south "31st parallel south"), and longitudes [27°](/wiki/27th_meridian_east "27th meridian east") and [30°E](/wiki/30th_meridian_east "30th meridian east"). About 12% of Lesotho is arable land which is vulnerable to [soil erosion](/wiki/Soil_erosion "Soil erosion"); it is estimated that 40 million tons of soil are lost each year due to erosion.[[58]](#cite_not

In his last days in office, President Tyler sought to complete the annexation of Texas. After the Senate had defeated an earlier treaty that required a two-thirds majority, Tyler urged Congress to pass a joint resolution, relying on its constitutional power to admit states.[[121]](#cite_note-Merry120124-123) There were disagreements about the terms under which Texas would be admitted and Polk became involved in negotiations to break the impasse. With Polk's help, the annexation resolution narrowly cleared the Senate.[[121]](#cite_note-Merry120124-123) Tyler was unsure whether to sign the resolution or leave it for Polk and sent Calhoun to consult with Polk, who declined to give any advice. On his final evening in office, March 3, 1845, Tyler offered annexation to Texas according to the terms of the resolution.[[122]](#cite_note-124)

Even before his inauguration, Polk wrote to Cave Johnson, "I intend to be *myself* President of the U.S."[[123]](#cite_note-125) He would gain a reputation as a hard worker, spending ten to twelve hours at his desk, and rarely leaving Washington. Polk wrote, "No President who performs his duty faithfully and conscientiously can have any leisure. I prefer to supervise the whole operations of the government myself rather than intrust the public business to subordinates, and this makes my duties very great."[[3]](#cite_note-a-3) When he took office on March 4, 1845, Polk, at 49, became the [youngest president](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age") to that point. But the spirit of adventure is not there any more. It is lost. There are people going up there who have no idea how to put on [crampons](/wiki/Crampons "Crampons"). One example of this is [Shriya Shah-Klorfine](/wiki/Shriya_Shah-Klorfine "Shriya Shah-Klorfine"), who had to be taught how to put on crampons during her summit attempt in 2012.[[242]](#cite_note-250) She paid at least US$40,000 to a new guiding company for the trip, and died when she ran out of oxygen during the descent after climbing for 27 hours straight.[[243]](#cite_note-251)

[Reinhold Messner](/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") concurred in 2004:

> You could die in each climb and that meant you were responsible for yourself. We were real mountaineers: careful, aware and even afraid. By climbing mountains we were not learning how big we were. I have always said that a mountain without danger is not a mountain....High altitude alpinism has become tourism and show. These commercial trips to Everest, they are still dangerous. Shanghai has a [humid subtropical climate](/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") ([Köppen](/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): *Cfa*), with an average annual temperature of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) for downtown areas and 16.2–17.2 °C (61.2–63.0 °F) for suburbs.[[67]](#cite_note-SHChroniclesEnvir-73) The city experiences four distinct seasons. Winters are temperate to cold and damp—northwesterly winds from [Siberia](/wiki/Siberia "Siberia") can cause nighttime temperatures to drop below freezing. Each year, there are an average of 4.7 days with snowfall and 1.6 days with snow cover.[[67]](#cite_note-SHChroniclesEnvir-73) Summers are hot and humid, and occasional downpours or [thunderstorms](/wiki/Thunderstorms "Thunderstorms") can be expected. On average, 14.5 days exceed 35 °C (95 °F) annually. In summer and the beginning of autumn, the city is susceptible to [typhoons](/wiki/Typhoon "Typhoon").[[73]](#cite_note-wiphatelegraph-79)

The most pleasant seasons are generally spring, although changeable and often rainy, and autumn, which is usually sunny and dry. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in June to 46% in August, the city receives 1,754 hours of bright sunshine annually.[[g]](#cite_note-80) According to China's seasonal division standard, from 2001 to 2025, Shanghai enters spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, and winter on 4 December. The average temperature for the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August is above 30 °C (86.0 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977 (unofficial record of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was set on 19 January 1893) to 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) on 21 July 2017[[74]](#cite_note-81) and 13 July 2022[[75]](#cite_note-82) at a [weather station](/wiki/Weather_station "Weather station") in [Xujiahui](/wiki/Xujiahui "Xujiahui").
